I am 72 years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou County for more than fifty years. I never went to school, but I know this land and the seasons better than any book. My family has about six mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. My son works in Handan city, so I manage the day-to-day work myself, though he comes back to help with harvest. Around here, if you want to eat and have grain left to sell, you grow winter wheat and summer maize on the same land. That is what I have always done, and that is what I will do this year.

My wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October after rotary tilling the maize stubble. I planted **Jimai 22**, an improved variety that my neighbors and I have trusted for years. It is hardy and gives steady yields. Before sowing, I spread one bag of compound fertilizer per mu as basal. Now that spring has come, I will topdress with urea at green-up and again at jointing stage. Wheat is thirsty, so I will irrigate three times: at green-up, jointing, and grain filling. I also need to spray pesticides four times in total — herbicide once to control weeds, insecticide twice for aphids and armyworms, and fungicide once to prevent rust. I expect about 1,000 jin per mu, which is 500 kg.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will sow **Denghai 605** maize the same day or the next day. We stopped ploughing for maize years ago — we just no-till plant straight into the wheat stubble. It saves diesel, time, and labor, and the yield is just as good. I will put down compound fertilizer at sowing. Maize does not need as much water as wheat, so two irrigations will be enough: one when the plants are about knee-high, and one at tasseling. I will spray insecticide and herbicide two or three times total to keep the pests down. I expect about 1,100 jin per mu, which is 550 kg.

This is the system my father taught me, and it has fed my family every year.
